title: Latency drift incident review and customer handoff - 2025-03
content:
Summary:

This doc captures the investigation into a customer-facing latency drift observed on 2025-03-09 affecting the nimbledocs route (hosted API). The customer reported intermittent P95/P99 regressions (from ~120ms to 400–700ms) over a ~6 hour window. We validated SLO misses for that route and executed a hotfix which reduced observed latencies to baseline. This is an internal review and the notes we handed off to CS for customer communication.

High-level impact:
- Affected tenant(s): nimbledocs (multi-tenant hosted lane)
- Window: 2025-03-09 09:12 UTC -> 2025-03-09 15:30 UTC (saw residual noise until 2025-03-10)
- SLO impact: P95 exceeded SLA by ~3–5x during peaks, P99s peaked at ~1s for some short bursts
- Error budget: small but visible; page triggered and CS escalated at 09:45 UTC

Initial hypothesis (from on-call):
- A sudden change in request shape or sequence length distribution caused a batching/kv-cache interaction that increased per-token overhead.
- Possible continuous-batching behavior interacting with our new coalescing heuristic (merged small requests into larger batches) causing head-of-line delays.

Timeline (key events):
- 2025-03-09 09:12 UTC: Customer report - higher latency on nimbledocs route.
- 09:18 UTC: On-call triage - confirmed metric spike in p95/p99 in datadog dashboards for the route.
- 09:25 UTC: Hot-path collection enabled (trace-level + sample profiler) for instances serving nimbledocs.
- 09:40 UTC: Temporary traffic-shift rule applied to route to reduce concurrency per instance (mitigation 1).
- 10:05 UTC: Initial flamegraphs and kernel timelines show long idle gaps between batch dispatch and GPU kernel start (queueing/serialization).
- 10:20 UTC: Identified recent config change rolled out 2025-03-08 that enabled aggressive request coalescing (PR #1839).
- 10:45 UTC: Hotfix applied: revert coalescing heuristic and set batching.backoff_ms from 8 -> 2 for affected pool (hotfix PR #1864).
- 11:10 UTC: Observed drop in p95/p99 to near-baseline for most customers.
- 15:30 UTC: Full rollback validated on all zones; follow-up rollout scheduled to reintroduce a safer variant of the feature behind a stronger canary.

What we profiled and how:
- Tools used: sampling profiler (built-in runtime sampler), perf on CPU-side worker threads, device traces (Nsight/Trace) on a repro rig, and internal request tracing (span-level).
- Artifacts collected: CPU flamegraphs (10s samples), GPU kernel timeline screenshots, request-level traces with batch composition metadata, kv-cache hit/miss counters, and runtime batching logs. Links in linked_artifacts.
- Key observation: batches contained many heterogeneous sequences (mix of short & long) leading to KV cache thrashing and longer prefix handling time on host-side before kernel dispatch. The host-side batching loop had an O(n) concatenation path for small requests that became hot under coalesced workloads.

Root cause (short form):
- The aggressive coalescing heuristic (merged small in-flight requests to build larger, presumably more GPU-efficient batches) interacted poorly with our prefix/KV cache eviction policy. When many small requests were merged, the effective sequence-length variance increased, causing extra CPU work in sequence prep and higher memory pressure on the KV cache. This produced both host-side serialization delays and intermittent extra device kernel stalls due to less cache-friendly memory layout.

Detailed root cause evidence:
- Trace-level example (req ids redacted): batch #4521 shows 18 requests merged; host preproc time = 210ms (baseline 20–40ms), GPU kernel queue wait = 120ms.
- CPU flamegraphs: top hot functions were batch_coalesce(), kv_cache_lookup(), and serialize_prefixes() — batch_coalesce accounted for ~38% of active CPU samples during spike window.
- NVTX timelines: several kernels started later than expected; gaps aligned with host-side serialization windows.
- Config audit: PR #1839 enabled coalescing with default window 30ms; rollout targeted dedicated pools but accidentally included hosted nimbledocs lane due to label mismatch.

Mitigations taken (and validation):
1) Immediate mitigation: revert coalescing heuristic on hosted pool (hotfix PR #1864). Rollout: canary -> 100% in 20 minutes. Validation: Datadog p95 decreased to baseline within 45 minutes of canary.
2) Secondary mitigation: reduce batching.backoff_ms to lower aggregation window to minimize heterogeneity.
3) Traffic isolation: temporarily applied routing rule to prefer dedicated pool for heavy nimbledocs workloads until patch validated.
4) Added temporary telemetry: log batch composition (sequence-length histogram per batch) at 1% sample rate for the next 72 hours.

Hotfix validation notes:
- Validation harness: synthetic replay of observed request mix on staging cluster (same model version, same quantization) with exact sequence-length distribution. We replayed 30k requests across 12 instances and measured p50/p95/p99 before/after revert.
- Results: p95 improved by ~2.8x in replay after revert. p99 tail behavior improved but still shows a small long tail under intentionally extreme heterogeneity (actionable but low-impact).
- Customer-facing validation: we coordinated with CS to run two short customer-originated workloads; both passed with no observable throttling and acceptable latency.

Action items and owners (short):
- Aaron Chen: write a safer coalescing implementation that accounts for sequence-length variance (due 2025-04-02).
- Priya Kapoor: add unit/integration tests to ensure hosted vs dedicated pool label scoping during feature rollouts (due 2025-03-25).
- Liam O'Connor: implement batch composition telemetry into runtime and ship to prod at low sample rate (due 2025-03-20).
- Diego Morales: schedule a red-team-style stress test for coalescing features on staging (due 2025-03-28).
- Maya (owner): coordinate CS message and close ticket JIRA-INC-3472 (due 2025-03-17).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Is there a principled way to compute when coalescing helps vs harms given observed distribution? Can we auto-tune per-route? (research item)
- Should coalescing be enabled only on dedicated pools where we can control request shape? (policy decision for product)
- Are there further micro-optimizations to serialize_prefixes() to reduce O(n) behavior? (engineering spike)

Customer communication (handoff to CS):
- Short summary for customer: We observed an interaction between a new batching heuristic and our cache/serialization logic that temporarily increased latency for certain mixed workloads. We reverted the heuristic for hosted lanes and validated latency returned to normal. We are building a safer implementation and additional observability; CS may offer to run the customer on a dedicated lane or share expected rollout dates.
- Suggested content: apology, explanation in non-technical terms (batching heuristic -> worse mixing of short/long requests -> increased work -> brief latency), bullets on immediate fix + long-term plan, and offer for 1:1 review with eng (if customer wants).

Appendix (quick commands & artifacts):
- Profiling commands used (example):
  - runtime-sampler --route nimbledocs --duration 600 --out flame_20250309.svg
  - perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> && perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > perf_flame.svg
  - nvprof --profile-from-start off --metrics achieved_occupancy -- ./repro_binary
- Key artifacts: flame_20250309.svg, nvtx-timeline-0310.png, pr-1864 (hotfix), jira INC-3472.
- Repro notes: to reproduce we used a locally constructed request mixer using observed seq-length histogram from telemetry (available in confluence:latency-drift-2025-03).

Notes to self (informal):
- Okay to reintroduce smarter coalescing but need to gate by max-seq-variance and limit merged-request-count.
- We were lucky the label mismatch allowed this to leak to hosted; add rollout safety guard ASAP.
- Remember: latency SLOs for hosted API need extra conservative heuristics vs dedicated pools.

Document history: rough, created during post-incident triage. Will update after engineering spike and final CS message.
